course.title: Arabic: Foundations
course.description: A beginner's introduction to Arabic, taught entirely in English: what Arabic is and where it is spoken, the right-to-left cursive script, the consonants and the short and long vowels, essential greetings, numbers, and the elegant root-and-pattern system that generates whole families of words. Background and examples are drawn from the article on Arabic in Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), and every Arabic example is paired with a plain transliteration and its English meaning. The course closes with the place of Arabic in literature and world history.

questions.prompt: In which direction is Arabic written and read?
questions.explanation: Arabic runs right to left across the page, the opposite of English - see 'The Arabic script: right to left and cursive'.

questions.prompt: The formal, shared variety of Arabic used in writing, news, and formal speech is called...
options: Modern Standard Arabic, known as Fusha
questions.explanation: Modern Standard Arabic, called Fusha, is the common literary standard, while everyday speech uses regional dialects - see 'What Arabic is: Fusha and the dialects'.

questions.prompt: How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet?
questions.explanation: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters, nearly all of them consonants - see 'The alphabet: the consonants'.

questions.prompt: Arabic script is best described as...
options: cursive, with letters that join to their neighbors
a set of pictures of objects
the same shape in every position
questions.explanation: Arabic is cursive: letters connect, and most change shape depending on their position in the word.

questions.prompt: Short vowels in ordinary Arabic text are usually...
options: written as full-size letters every time
shown by small marks that are often left out
questions.explanation: Short vowels are small diacritical marks that skilled readers usually supply from context, so most everyday text omits them.
It literally means 'peace be upon you' and is the most common Arabic greeting - see the greetings vocabulary lesson.

questions.prompt: Most Arabic words are built on a core made of how many consonants?
questions.explanation: The typical root is three consonants, and patterns wrapped around that root create related words - see 'Roots, patterns, and building sentences'.

questions.prompt: Arabic is an official or co-official language across which broad region?
options: the Middle East and North Africa
questions.explanation: Arabic is spoken across the Middle East and North Africa by hundreds of millions of people - see 'What Arabic is: Fusha and the dialects'.

lessons.title: What Arabic is: Fusha and the dialects
lessons.grammar_note: There is no single spoken Arabic; the written standard (Fusha) and the everyday dialects coexist, a situation linguists call diglossia.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what Arabic is, name the broad region where it is spoken, and explain the difference between Modern Standard Arabic (called Fusha) and the many regional dialects. Warm-up: if a newsreader in Cairo and a newsreader in Rabat both read the same bulletin, they use one shared form of the language - but at home with family they might speak quite differently. How can both be 'Arabic'? This is one of the first things that surprises beginners, and understanding it early will save you confusion later. According to Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, Arabic is a Semitic language with a very large number of speakers, and the gap between its formal written form and its local spoken forms is a defining feature of how the language actually works day to day.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Arabic is a Semitic language, related to Hebrew and Amharic, spoken as a first language by hundreds of millions of people across the Middle East and North Africa, from Morocco in the west to the Arabian Peninsula and Iraq in the east. It is also the liturgical language of Islam, so it is read and recited far beyond that region. The key thing to grasp is that 'Arabic' names two layers at once. Modern Standard Arabic, called al-Fusha, is the shared formal variety used in writing, news broadcasts, books, and formal speeches; it is understood everywhere and is what this course teaches. Alongside it live the regional dialects (al-ammiyya), such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, and Maghrebi Arabic, which people actually speak at home and in the street. These dialects differ in vocabulary and pronunciation and are not always mutually understandable, yet all educated speakers share Fusha as a common standard. Learning Fusha gives you the key that fits every door.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: A few orienting words, each with a transliteration and its English meaning. The language itself: العربية (al-arabiyya) = Arabic. The formal standard: الفصحى (al-fusha) = the clear or eloquent form, Modern Standard Arabic. Everyday speech: العامية (al-ammiyya) = the common or colloquial speech, the dialects. The greeting that opens almost any conversation: السلام عليكم (as-salamu alaykum) = peace be upon you. A simple hello: مرحبا (marhaban) = hello, welcome. Notice that each Arabic word is given right to left, then a plain Latin-letter transliteration so you can say it, then the meaning - we will keep this three-part habit throughout, because the script is unfamiliar at first. Try reading each transliteration aloud: al-arabiyya, al-fusha, al-ammiyya, as-salamu alaykum, marhaban. The repeated element 'al' is simply the word 'the', attached to the front of the noun, and you will meet it constantly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check yourself. 1) Which form of Arabic would a television news anchor use for a formal bulletin? 2) True or false: the dialects spoken in Morocco and Iraq are always perfectly understandable to each other. 3) What family of languages does Arabic belong to? 4) What does the attached element 'al' mean in al-arabiyya? 5) Give the transliteration and meaning of السلام عليكم. Answers: 1) Modern Standard Arabic, Fusha, because it is the shared formal standard. 2) false - the dialects can differ enough that speakers from distant regions may not fully understand one another, which is exactly why Fusha matters. 3) the Semitic family, alongside Hebrew and Amharic. 4) it means 'the', so al-arabiyya is literally 'the Arabic'. 5) as-salamu alaykum, meaning 'peace be upon you'.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming there is one single spoken Arabic that everyone uses at home - in reality the written standard and the local dialects coexist, a split linguists call diglossia. Mistake: thinking Fusha is a dead or purely ancient form - Modern Standard Arabic is very much alive in print and broadcasting today. Mistake: expecting that learning one dialect lets you read a newspaper, or that learning Fusha lets you chat casually in a village; each layer has its own place, and this course builds the Fusha foundation first. Exit ticket: (a) What is the short Arabic name for Modern Standard Arabic? (b) Name two regions where Arabic is widely spoken. (c) What does the term diglossia describe? Answers: al-Fusha; for example Egypt and the Arabian Peninsula (Morocco, the Levant, and Iraq also count); the coexistence of a formal written standard with everyday spoken dialects.

lessons.title: The Arabic script: right to left and cursive
lessons.grammar_note: Arabic letters are cursive and join to their neighbors, so most letters take up to four shapes - initial, medial, final, and isolated - depending on where they sit in the word.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe three defining features of the Arabic writing system: that it runs right to left, that it is cursive with joined letters, and that most letters change shape according to their position in the word. Warm-up: in English handwriting we often join letters too, but the printed letter 'a' looks the same wherever it appears. What if a printed letter changed its shape depending on whether it began, sat inside, or ended a word? That is exactly how Arabic works, and it is the single biggest adjustment for a new reader. Once you expect the shape-shifting instead of being surprised by it, the script becomes far less intimidating and starts to feel like a connected, flowing line rather than a wall of unfamiliar symbols.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Three features define the script. First, direction: Arabic is written and read from right to left, so the first letter of a word sits on the right and the line fills toward the left. Numbers, interestingly, are written left to right within that right-to-left text. Second, it is cursive: even in print the letters connect to their neighbors with joining strokes, so a word is usually one continuous stroke rather than separate blocks. Third, because letters join, most of them take different shapes depending on position. A letter has up to four forms: an initial form (joined to what follows), a medial form (joined on both sides), a final form (joined to what precedes), and an isolated form (standing alone). A small group of letters only ever join on their right side, so they never connect to the letter after them; these are the non-connectors, and they create natural breaks even inside a single word. Spaces still separate words, as in English.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Take the common letter ب, whose name is 'ba' and which sounds like English b. In isolation it is ب. At the start of a word it becomes بـ (initial), in the middle ـبـ (medial), and at the end ـب (final) - the little connecting tails show where it links to its neighbors. You can see the same body with a single dot below it throughout; only the joining strokes change. Now a whole word: بيت (bayt) = house, read right to left as ba, ya, ta. Another: كتب (kataba) = he wrote, read right to left as kaf, ta, ba, with the letters flowing into one another. Compare the non-connector ا (alif), which joins only on its right: in دار (dar) = house or home, the alif links to the letter before it but leaves a small gap before the next letter. Say each aloud: bayt, kataba, dar, and trace the direction with your finger from right to left.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) In which direction do you read the letters of an Arabic word? 2) How many shapes can a typical Arabic letter take, and what are they called? 3) In the word بيت (bayt), which side of the word does the first letter sit on? 4) What is special about a non-connector such as ا (alif)? 5) Within right-to-left text, which direction are numerals written? Answers: 1) right to left, starting from the right-hand side. 2) up to four - initial, medial, final, and isolated - depending on position. 3) the right side, since Arabic begins on the right. 4) it joins only to the letter on its right, so it never connects to the letter that follows it, leaving a small break. 5) numerals run left to right even inside right-to-left text.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to read Arabic left to right out of habit - always begin on the right. Mistake: expecting a letter to look identical everywhere, then failing to recognize it in its joined forms; remember that ب isolated and ـبـ in the middle are the same letter. Mistake: assuming every letter connects on both sides - the non-connectors join only on the right, so a word can show gaps that are not spaces between words. Exit ticket: (a) Which direction does Arabic text flow? (b) Name the four position-based forms a letter can take. (c) Why do some single words contain small internal gaps? Answers: right to left; initial, medial, final, and isolated; because a non-connector letter refuses to join the letter that follows it, creating a break inside the word.

lessons.title: The alphabet: the consonants
lessons.grammar_note: The 28 letters stand mainly for consonants; dots placed above or below an otherwise identical body distinguish many letters from one another.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say how many letters the Arabic alphabet has, explain that it records mainly consonants, and recognize how dots distinguish letters that share the same basic body. Warm-up: imagine an alphabet where several letters are drawn with the exact same curve, and the only thing telling them apart is one dot above, two dots below, or three dots on top. How carefully would you have to look? Arabic asks exactly that of you, and the good news is that learning one body-shape often unlocks three or four letters at once. This lesson gives you the lay of the land rather than drilling all 28 letters, so that when you meet them in full you already understand the logic holding the alphabet together.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters, and nearly all of them are consonants. Three letters double as carriers of the long vowels, which we meet in the next lesson, but the system is fundamentally a consonantal one: it writes the skeleton of consonants and lets the reader supply most of the vowels. A striking feature is that many letters share one identical body and are told apart only by dots, called nuqat. For example, the same tooth-shaped body becomes ب (ba, the b sound) with one dot below, ت (ta, the t sound) with two dots above, and ث (tha, as in 'think') with three dots above. Likewise ج (jim, a j sound), ح (ha, a deep breathy h), and خ (kha, a rasping sound like the ch in 'Bach') share one body distinguished by a dot's presence and position. Learning the families of shapes, rather than 28 isolated symbols, makes the alphabet far more manageable.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Here are the first several letters with their names, their sounds, and a sample word, each Arabic example followed by a transliteration and English meaning. ا (alif) carries the long 'aa' sound, as in باب (bab) = door. ب (ba) is b, as in بيت (bayt) = house. ت (ta) is t, as in تمر (tamr) = dates, the fruit. ث (tha) is the soft 'th' in 'think', as in ثلاثة (thalatha) = three. ج (jim) is j, as in جمل (jamal) = camel. ح (ha) is a strong, breathy h made deep in the throat, as in حليب (halib) = milk. د (dal) is d, as in درس (dars) = lesson. ر (ra) is a rolled r, as in رجل (rajul) = man. Say the names in order: alif, ba, ta, tha, jim, ha, dal, ra. Notice how ba, ta, and tha share one body and differ only in their dots.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet? 2) The alphabet records mainly which type of sound? 3) What single visual feature tells ب, ت, and ث apart? 4) Give the sound and a sample word for the letter ج (jim). 5) Which letter carries the long 'aa' vowel sound? Answers: 1) 28 letters. 2) consonants - the vowels are mostly left for the reader to supply. 3) the dots (nuqat): one dot below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha, all on the same body. 4) jim is a j sound, as in جمل (jamal) = camel. 5) ا (alif) carries the long 'aa', as in باب (bab) = door.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating each letter as a wholly new shape to memorize, instead of learning body-shapes in families and letting the dots do the sorting. Mistake: ignoring the dots, which are not decoration - missing or misreading a dot turns one letter into another and changes the word. Mistake: expecting the alphabet to spell out every vowel; it marks consonants and long vowels, while short vowels are usually left out. Exit ticket: (a) How many letters does Arabic have? (b) What are the small marks called that distinguish same-bodied letters? (c) Name the three letters that share the tooth-shaped body ب ت ث and their distinguishing dots. Answers: 28; the dots, or nuqat; ba with one dot below, ta with two dots above, and tha with three dots above.

items.translation: as-salamu alaykum - peace be upon you (the standard greeting)
items.example: A speaker enters a room and says السلام عليكم (as-salamu alaykum) to greet everyone.

items.translation: wa alaykum as-salam - and upon you be peace (the reply)
items.example: The reply to the greeting is وعليكم السلام (wa alaykum as-salam), 'and peace be upon you too'.
A friendly, everyday hello is simply مرحبا (marhaban).

items.translation: sabah al-khayr - good morning (literally 'morning of goodness')
items.example: In the morning you say صباح الخير (sabah al-khayr), good morning.

items.translation: masa al-khayr - good evening (literally 'evening of goodness')
items.example: Later in the day you say مساء الخير (masa al-khayr), good evening.
To thank someone you say شكرا (shukran), thank you.
To ask politely you add من فضلك (min fadlik), please.
On leaving you say مع السلامة (ma a as-salama), goodbye.
To agree you say نعم (na am), yes.
To decline you say لا (la), no.

lessons.title: Short and long vowels, diacritics, and distinctive sounds
lessons.grammar_note: Short vowels are small marks above or below a consonant and are usually omitted; long vowels are written with the letters alif, waw, and ya.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name the three short vowels and the three long vowels of Arabic, explain why short vowels are usually left out of ordinary text, and recognize a few sounds that have no close English equivalent. Warm-up: if you saw the English word 'bt' with no vowels, could you tell whether it means 'bat', 'bit', 'but', or 'bet'? You would use context. Arabic readers do exactly this every day, because most text writes only consonants and long vowels and leaves the short vowels to be filled in from knowledge of the word and the sentence. Understanding this is what lets you move from spelling out letters to actually reading, and it also explains why beginner and sacred texts add the little vowel marks that everyday newspapers drop.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Arabic has three short vowels, written as small diacritical marks on a consonant: fatha, a small stroke above, giving a short 'a'; kasra, a small stroke below, giving a short 'i'; and damma, a small loop above, giving a short 'u'. Each short vowel has a long partner, and the long vowels are written with full letters: alif ا for long 'aa', waw و for long 'uu', and ya ي for long 'ii'. A few other marks matter: sukun, a small circle, shows that a consonant has no vowel after it; shadda, a small w-shaped mark, doubles a consonant; and tanwin marks add an 'n' sound at the end of a word. In everyday writing the short-vowel marks are usually omitted, and the reader supplies them. They are written out in the Quran, in children's books, in dictionaries, and in language textbooks, precisely where removing ambiguity matters most. Arabic also has sounds with no close English match, made deep in the throat.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Short vowels on the letter ب (ba): بَ with fatha is 'ba', بِ with kasra is 'bi', بُ with damma is 'bu'. Long vowels stretch the sound: با is 'baa', بو is 'buu', بي is 'bii'. See the length difference in كَتَبَ (kataba) = he wrote, all short vowels, versus كاتِب (katib) = writer, with a long 'aa' in the first syllable. Now some distinctive consonants, each with a plain-English hint. ع (ayn) is a voiced sound made deep in the throat with no English equivalent, as in عَرَبِيّ (arabiyy) = Arab or Arabic. ح (ha) is a strong breathy h, as in حُبّ (hubb) = love. خ (kha) rasps like the ch in the composer's name 'Bach', as in خُبز (khubz) = bread. ق (qaf) is a k made far back in the throat, as in قَلب (qalb) = heart. Say them slowly: ayn, ha, kha, qaf.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Name the three short vowels and the sound each adds. 2) Which three letters carry the long vowels? 3) Why do most newspapers leave the short-vowel marks out? 4) What does the shadda mark do to a consonant? 5) Describe, in plain terms, the sound of ح (ha). Answers: 1) fatha gives short 'a', kasra gives short 'i', and damma gives short 'u'. 2) alif ا for long 'aa', waw و for long 'uu', and ya ي for long 'ii'. 3) skilled readers supply the short vowels from context, so the marks are treated as optional in ordinary text and reserved for places where clarity is essential. 4) the shadda doubles the consonant, so it is pronounced twice as long or with extra weight. 5) it is a strong, breathy h produced deep in the throat, firmer than the English h.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing short and long vowels - the long ones are twice the length and are written with full letters, and the difference can change a word, as with kataba (he wrote) versus katib (writer). Mistake: panicking at vowel-less text; remember that the short vowels are simply left for you to supply as your vocabulary grows. Mistake: pronouncing ع (ayn), ح (ha), خ (kha), and ق (qaf) as if they were plain English vowels or a simple k - they live deeper in the throat and need practice. Exit ticket: (a) How many short vowels does Arabic have, and what are they called? (b) Which letter writes the long 'uu' sound? (c) Which mark shows that a consonant carries no following vowel? Answers: three - fatha, kasra, and damma; the letter waw و; the sukun.

questions.prompt: Modern Standard Arabic, the shared formal written variety, is called...
questions.explanation: al-Fusha is Modern Standard Arabic; al-ammiyya refers to the everyday dialects.

questions.prompt: How many position-based shapes can a typical Arabic letter take?
questions.explanation: Because the script is cursive, a letter can have initial, medial, final, and isolated forms - up to four.

questions.prompt: Which small marks distinguish same-bodied letters such as ب, ت, and ث?
questions.explanation: The dots (nuqat) tell apart letters that share one body: one dot below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha.

questions.prompt: The short vowel 'kasra' is written as a small stroke below a consonant and gives which sound?
questions.explanation: Kasra, written below the letter, gives a short 'i'; fatha above gives 'a' and damma above gives 'u'.

questions.prompt: In ordinary Arabic writing, the short-vowel marks are...
options: usually omitted and supplied by the reader
questions.explanation: Everyday text leaves out the short-vowel marks; they appear in the Quran, children's books, dictionaries, and textbooks.

questions.prompt: The phrase 'as-salamu alaykum' is answered with...
questions.explanation: The standard reply reverses the greeting: wa alaykum as-salam, 'and upon you be peace'.

lessons.title: Roots, patterns, and building sentences
lessons.grammar_note: A typical Arabic word is a three-consonant root slotted into a vowel-and-affix pattern; a simple statement like 'the house is big' needs no verb 'to be'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain the root-and-pattern system that sits at the heart of Arabic word-building, use it to connect several related words, and form a very basic statement without needing a verb for 'to be'. Warm-up: in English, 'write', 'writer', 'written', and 'writing' clearly share a core. What if that shared core were a fixed trio of consonants, and you could pour it into standard molds to make each new word? That is precisely how Arabic generates vocabulary, and once you see the pattern you can often guess a word's meaning from its root. This is one of the most satisfying discoveries in beginning Arabic, because it turns a long list of separate words into a small set of roots multiplied by a small set of reliable patterns.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most Arabic words grow from a root of three consonants that carries a core meaning, placed into a pattern of vowels and occasional extra letters that shapes the grammar. The classic example is the root k-t-b, which has to do with writing. Pour it into different patterns and you get a whole family: the past-tense verb, the word for writer, the word for book, and the word for library or office, all recognizably sharing the same three consonants in the same order. Learning to spot the root lets you read a new word and guess its area of meaning, while the pattern tells you whether it is a verb, a doer, a place, or a thing. For simple sentences, Arabic often needs no verb for 'to be' in the present: to say 'the house is big' you simply place 'the house' next to 'big'. This is called a nominal or equational sentence, and it is the gentlest way into Arabic syntax.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: The root k-t-b (writing) across its family, each with transliteration and meaning: كَتَبَ (kataba) = he wrote; كاتِب (katib) = writer; كِتاب (kitab) = book; مَكتَبة (maktaba) = library; مَكتَب (maktab) = office or desk; مَكتوب (maktub) = written, or a letter. Notice the three consonants k, t, b sitting in order inside every one. Now basic sentences with no verb for 'to be': البَيت كَبير (al-bayt kabir) = the house is big, literally 'the house big'. هٰذا كِتاب (hadha kitab) = this is a book. أنا طالِب (ana talib) = I am a student. The little word أنا (ana) = I, and هٰذا (hadha) = this. Join what you know: هٰذا كِتاب كَبير (hadha kitab kabir) = this is a big book. Read each slowly, right to left, and find the root inside the longer words.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What three consonants form the root shared by kataba, kitab, and maktaba? 2) What general area of meaning does that root carry? 3) Translate البَيت كَبير (al-bayt kabir) and explain why it has no verb. 4) Using أنا (ana) and طالِب (talib), say 'I am a student'. 5) Which pattern word in the k-t-b family means 'library'? Answers: 1) k, t, and b, in that order. 2) writing - every word in the family relates to it. 3) 'the house is big'; Arabic forms present-tense equational sentences by placing subject and predicate side by side, with no word for 'is'. 4) أنا طالِب (ana talib), literally 'I student'. 5) مَكتَبة (maktaba) means library, built from k-t-b with a place-pattern.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to memorize every word separately instead of learning the root and recognizing the pattern wrapped around it. Mistake: inserting a word for 'is' into a simple present-tense statement - Arabic leaves it out, so 'the house big' is a complete sentence. Mistake: scrambling the order of the root consonants; k-t-b and a different order would point to a different meaning entirely, so keep the three consonants in sequence. Exit ticket: (a) How many consonants are in a typical Arabic root? (b) What does the k-t-b family of words have in common in meaning? (c) Does a present-tense sentence like 'the house is big' use a verb for 'to be'? Answers: three; they all relate to writing; no - the present-tense equational sentence has no verb for 'to be'.

items.example: كِتاب واحِد (kitab wahid) = one book.
بَيتان اثنان (baytan ithnan) = two houses.
ثَلاثة كُتُب (thalatha kutub) = three books.
أربَعة أيام (arba a ayyam) = four days.
خَمسة أولاد (khamsa awlad) = five boys.
عَشَرة دَنانير (ashara dananir) = ten dinars.
هٰذا بَيت كَبير (hadha bayt kabir) = this is a big house.
أُريد ماء (urid ma) = I want water.
الكِتاب جَديد (al-kitab jadid) = the book is new.
المَدرَسة قَريبة (al-madrasa qariba) = the school is near.

lessons.title: The place of Arabic in literature and world history
lessons.grammar_note: Arabic's spread as a language of scripture, scholarship, and trade made it one of the great carrier-languages of world knowledge, leaving loanwords in many languages including English.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain why Arabic matters far beyond its native speakers, name a few fields in which Arabic writing shaped world knowledge, and recognize some everyday English words that were borrowed from Arabic. Warm-up: when you say 'algebra', 'coffee', or 'sugar', you are already speaking a little Arabic - how do you think those words traveled into English? This closing lesson steps back from letters and grammar to see the bigger picture, because part of learning any language is understanding the civilization that carries it. According to Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, Arabic has served for many centuries as a major language of religion, science, philosophy, and literature, and that history is still visible in the vocabulary of languages spoken thousands of miles from the Arab world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Arabic rose to global importance for several reasons at once. As the language of the Quran it became, and remains, the liturgical language of Islam, recited and studied by well over a billion people. As the administrative and scholarly language of a vast medieval world stretching from Spain to Central Asia, it became the vehicle for enormous advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine, geography, and philosophy, and for the preservation and transmission of earlier Greek learning that might otherwise have been lost. Its literary tradition is equally deep, from pre-Islamic poetry to the famous story collection known in English as the 'Thousand and One Nights'. Through centuries of trade, scholarship, and contact across the Mediterranean, Arabic lent words to many languages. English alone absorbed a long list of them, often through Spanish, Italian, or Latin, so that scientific, commercial, and everyday vocabulary all carry an Arabic layer that most speakers never notice.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Several English words trace back to Arabic roots, each shown here with its Arabic source, a transliteration, and the meaning. 'Algebra' comes from الجَبر (al-jabr) = the restoring or reunion of broken parts, the name of a method in a famous mathematics text. 'Coffee' comes from قَهوة (qahwa) = coffee. 'Sugar' goes back to سُكَّر (sukkar) = sugar. 'Cotton' comes from قُطن (qutn) = cotton. 'Admiral' derives from أَمير (amir) = commander or prince. The common prefix in many of these, 'al', is simply the Arabic word for 'the', which rode along into English in words like 'algebra', 'alcohol', and 'algorithm'. Say the Arabic sources aloud: al-jabr, qahwa, sukkar, qutn, amir. Each one is a small bridge between the language you are learning and the language you already speak, and spotting them is a pleasant habit that will keep rewarding you.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Name two fields of knowledge that medieval Arabic scholarship advanced. 2) Which famous story collection is known in English as the 'Thousand and One Nights'? 3) From which Arabic word does English 'coffee' come? 4) What does the attached 'al' in 'algebra' originally mean? 5) Give one reason Arabic spread so widely beyond its original region. Answers: 1) for example mathematics and astronomy (medicine, geography, and philosophy also count). 2) the collection of tales often called in Arabic Alf Layla wa-Layla, the 'Thousand and One Nights'. 3) from قَهوة (qahwa), meaning coffee. 4) it means 'the', the Arabic definite article, carried along into the borrowed word. 5) because it became the language of Islamic scripture and of a vast realm of scholarship and trade, which carried it across continents.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining Arabic as a purely local or purely ancient language - it has been a world language of science and literature for well over a thousand years and remains widely spoken and written today. Mistake: assuming English and Arabic share nothing, when in fact English holds a quiet layer of Arabic loanwords in science, trade, and daily life. Mistake: forgetting that much classical Greek learning reached later Europe in part through Arabic translation and commentary. Exit ticket: (a) Name one English word borrowed from Arabic. (b) What does the element 'al' mean in such words? (c) Give one historical reason Arabic became so influential. Answers: for example algebra, coffee, sugar, cotton, or admiral; it means 'the', the definite article; its role as the language of scripture, scholarship, and trade across a vast medieval world.
